# Antennal Contact Regulation in Red Harvester Ants

## Colony Context Without Central Coordination

Colonies of the red harvester ant (*Pogonomyrmex barbatus*) operate in arid desert habitats where seed availability fluctuates rapidly over minutes to hours. Despite fielding thousands of active workers across foraging trails extending up to twenty meters from the nest, the colony possesses no central dispatcher, global inventory census, or hierarchical command chain. Each worker relies strictly on short-range local encounters inside the shallow entrance chamber just below the nest surface.

## Local Contact Rate Sensing and Leaky Integration

Harvester ant workers adjust their outgoing foraging rate based solely on brief antennal contact frequencies with returning food-bearing nestmates inside the entrance chamber. When a forager locates seeds, it returns carrying a seed and emits specific cuticular hydrocarbon cues that distinguish food-bearing returnees from unsuccessful patrollers or nest maintenance workers. Inactive reserve workers wait near the entrance tunnel and integrate incoming antennal contacts over a short leaky temporal window of roughly ten to twenty seconds.

Because contacts are physical touch events lasting less than half a second, each waiting worker estimates local foraging success without observing distant trails or total colony food stores. The individual probability or outflow rate of a waiting reserve worker switching into active foraging follows a sigmoidal activation curve around a worker-specific threshold $\theta_i$:

$$R_{\text{out}}(t) = R_{\max} \cdot \frac{1}{1 + \exp\!\left(-\beta \left(f_{\text{food}}(t) - \theta_i\right)\right)}$$

Here $f_{\text{food}}(t)$ denotes the exponentially weighted moving frequency of antennal contacts with seed-carrying returnees, $\beta$ sets the steepness of recruitment sensitivity, and $\theta_i$ represents the heterogeneous activation threshold of worker $i$. Heterogeneous thresholds prevent all idle workers from rushing out simultaneously on a single noisy burst.

## Self-Limiting Shutdown Under Resource Depletion or Predation

When external seed patches become depleted or when predators disrupt returning foragers, the arrival rate of seed-bearing ants at the nest entrance drops immediately. Because the local contact integrator decays exponentially in the absence of fresh contacts, $f_{\text{food}}(t)$ falls below $\theta_i$ and outgoing recruitment shuts down automatically without requiring any global stop broadcast. Conversely, a sudden windfall of seeds increases return frequency and scales up active foragers within minutes while keeping energy expenditure bounded when conditions are poor.

# Decentralized Edge Cluster Autoscaling Under Intermittent Connectivity

## Architectural Bottlenecks of Centralized Control Planes

Modern industrial IoT and autonomous telemetry deployments run containerized inference and stream-processing jobs across hundreds of distributed edge compute nodes located in factories, substations, and mobile gateways. Traditional autoscalers such as centralized Horizontal Pod Autoscalers rely on periodic metric scraping into a single cloud control plane, followed by centralized scheduling and replica-count commands.

Under bursty local sensor workloads and intermittent WAN links experiencing 400 ms to 2500 ms round-trip latency or complete network partitions, centralized edge autoscalers suffer severe control-plane lag and split-brain oscillation. When the WAN link drops during a local workload spike, edge clusters cannot reach the cloud master to request scale-out capacity, causing local request queues to overflow and critical telemetry frames to be dropped.

## Constraints for Autonomous Node-Level Admission and Scale-Out

Each edge cluster site contains a pool of low-power worker nodes that keep idle runtime containers in a suspended warm-standby state to conserve battery and thermal headroom. Because nodes lack reliable global cluster state during WAN partitions and cannot afford high-overhead consensus protocols on constrained wireless backhauls, each node must decide autonomously when to wake standby worker replicas or shed incoming bursts.

Existing threshold-based local PID controllers fail when burst arrivals are noisy: if every standby node wakes simultaneously on a brief queue spike, power draw exceeds the site thermal envelope and triggers thrashing. What is required is a lightweight, purely local activation mechanism in which nodes exchange brief peer-to-peer completion receipts with neighboring workers, integrate successful job-completion contact rates over a decaying time window, and activate staggered standby capacity without any central monitor.
